title: Metabolism of Amino Acids & Protein
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Metabolism of Amino Acids and Protein curriculum: transamination/deamination, ammonia transport and the urea cycle, glucogenic/ketogenic amino acid catabolism, specific amino acid pathways and their inborn errors, protein turnover, nitrogen balance, and essential/non-essential amino acid classification. Scope is amino acid/protein nitrogen metabolism specifically, kept distinct from lipid, carbohydrate, and nucleic acid metabolism courses.

questions.question: Transamination reactions, which transfer an amino group from an amino acid to an alpha-keto acid, universally require which coenzyme?
questions.explanation: All aminotransferases (transaminases) use pyridoxal-5'-phosphate, derived from vitamin B6, as an essential coenzyme that forms a Schiff base intermediate to shuttle the amino group between substrates.

questions.question: Alanine aminotransferase catalyzes the transfer of an amino group from alanine to alpha-ketoglutarate, producing:
questions.explanation: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) transfers alanine's amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate, yielding pyruvate (alanine's carbon skeleton) and glutamate, which channels amino groups toward the urea cycle or further deamination.

questions.question: Glutamate dehydrogenase, a key enzyme linking amino acid nitrogen to free ammonia, catalyzes oxidative deamination of glutamate using which coenzyme(s)?
questions.explanation: Glutamate dehydrogenase, located in the mitochondrial matrix, oxidatively deaminates glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate and free ammonia, using either NAD+ or NADP+ as electron acceptor, and is allosterically regulated by ATP/GTP (inhibitory) and ADP (stimulatory).

questions.question: Why is glutamate considered the central 'collecting point' for amino groups prior to urea synthesis?
options: Because most aminotransferases funnel amino groups from diverse amino acids onto alpha-ketoglutarate, forming glutamate, which glutamate dehydrogenase can then deaminate
Because glutamate cannot be converted to any other molecule
Because only glutamate can enter the mitochondria
Because glutamate is the only amino acid that is glucogenic
questions.correct_answer: Because most aminotransferases funnel amino groups from diverse amino acids onto alpha-ketoglutarate, forming glutamate, which glutamate dehydrogenase can then deaminate
questions.explanation: Because a wide range of aminotransferases use alpha-ketoglutarate/glutamate as their common amino-group acceptor/donor pair, amino groups from many different amino acids converge on glutamate, which is then oxidatively deaminated to release free ammonia for urea synthesis.

questions.question: In skeletal muscle, excess amino group nitrogen is transported to the liver mainly in the non-toxic form of:
options: Alanine (via the glucose-alanine cycle) and glutamine
questions.correct_answer: Alanine (via the glucose-alanine cycle) and glutamine
questions.explanation: Muscle transaminates amino groups onto pyruvate to form alanine (glucose-alanine cycle) or onto glutamate to form glutamine, both non-toxic carriers that transport nitrogen safely through the blood to the liver (and glutamine also to the kidney).

questions.question: Glutamine synthetase, which combines glutamate and free ammonia to form glutamine, functions physiologically to:
options: Detoxify ammonia in tissues (especially brain and muscle) by incorporating it into a safely transportable amino acid
questions.correct_answer: Detoxify ammonia in tissues (especially brain and muscle) by incorporating it into a safely transportable amino acid
questions.explanation: Glutamine synthetase uses ATP to condense free ammonia with glutamate, forming glutamine; this is a major route for temporarily detoxifying ammonia, particularly important in the brain, which is highly sensitive to ammonia toxicity.

questions.question: The first, committed, mitochondrial-matrix enzyme of the urea cycle, which condenses ammonia, bicarbonate, and ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate, is:
questions.explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I), located in liver mitochondria, catalyzes the rate-limiting first step of the urea cycle, using 2 ATP to combine free ammonia and bicarbonate into carbamoyl phosphate; it requires N-acetylglutamate as an allosteric activator.

questions.question: N-acetylglutamate is an essential allosteric activator of which urea cycle enzyme?
questions.explanation: N-acetylglutamate, synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate in response to rising amino acid/ammonia levels, is an obligatory allosteric activator of CPS I, coupling ureagenesis to amino acid intake.

questions.question: Ornithine transcarbamoylase catalyzes the reaction that combines carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form:
questions.explanation: Ornithine transcarbamoylase, a mitochondrial matrix enzyme, transfers the carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate onto ornithine, producing citrulline, which is then transported to the cytosol for the remaining urea cycle steps.

questions.question: In the urea cycle, the second nitrogen atom of urea is introduced when citrulline condenses with aspartate to form argininosuccinate, catalyzed by:
questions.explanation: Argininosuccinate synthetase, in the cytosol, condenses citrulline with aspartate (using ATP) to form argininosuccinate, incorporating the second nitrogen of urea, which is derived from aspartate.

questions.question: Argininosuccinate lyase cleaves argininosuccinate into arginine and:
questions.explanation: Argininosuccinate lyase splits argininosuccinate into arginine (which continues in the cycle) and fumarate, which can enter the TCA cycle, linking the urea cycle to central carbon metabolism.

questions.question: The final step of the urea cycle, in which arginine is hydrolyzed to release urea and regenerate ornithine, is catalyzed by:
questions.explanation: Arginase hydrolyzes arginine to urea and ornithine, completing the cycle; ornithine is transported back into the mitochondria to accept another carbamoyl phosphate and begin a new cycle.

questions.question: A deficiency of ornithine transcarbamoylase (OTC), the most common inherited urea cycle disorder, leads to accumulation of which toxic metabolite?
options: Ammonia (and excess orotic acid, as carbamoyl phosphate backs up into pyrimidine synthesis)
questions.correct_answer: Ammonia (and excess orotic acid, as carbamoyl phosphate backs up into pyrimidine synthesis)
questions.explanation: OTC deficiency blocks conversion of carbamoyl phosphate to citrulline, causing hyperammonemia (impaired urea synthesis) and, distinctively, excess carbamoyl phosphate diverted into the cytosolic pyrimidine pathway, raising urinary orotic acid.

questions.question: Amino acids are classified as 'glucogenic' when their carbon skeletons are catabolized to:
options: Pyruvate or a TCA cycle intermediate that can be converted to oxaloacetate and then to glucose via gluconeogenesis
questions.correct_answer: Pyruvate or a TCA cycle intermediate that can be converted to oxaloacetate and then to glucose via gluconeogenesis
questions.explanation: Glucogenic amino acids yield carbon skeletons (pyruvate or TCA cycle intermediates such as alpha-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, fumarate, oxaloacetate) that can be converted to oxaloacetate and used for gluconeogenesis.

questions.question: Leucine is unusual among the standard amino acids in being classified as:
questions.explanation: Leucine is catabolized entirely to acetyl-CoA and acetoacetate, with no net carbon entering gluconeogenesis, making it (along with lysine) one of the two purely ketogenic amino acids.

questions.question: Phenylketonuria (PKU) results from a deficiency of:
questions.explanation: PKU is caused by deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase (or its cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin), blocking conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine; phenylalanine and its byproducts accumulate, causing severe intellectual disability if untreated.

questions.question: Dietary management of phenylketonuria centres on restricting phenylalanine intake while ensuring adequate:
questions.explanation: Because PKU blocks phenylalanine's conversion to tyrosine, tyrosine becomes a conditionally essential amino acid that must be supplied in the diet, alongside strict limitation of phenylalanine.

questions.question: Alkaptonuria, characterized by urine that darkens on standing and later joint cartilage pigmentation (ochronosis), is caused by a deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Alkaptonuria results from deficient homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase in the tyrosine degradation pathway, causing accumulation and urinary excretion of homogentisic acid, which darkens on air exposure and deposits in cartilage over time.

questions.question: Maple syrup urine disease results from a deficiency in the enzyme that oxidatively decarboxylates the branched-chain alpha-keto acids derived from:
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease is caused by deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase, a mitochondrial complex analogous to pyruvate dehydrogenase, which is required for catabolism of leucine, isoleucine, and valine; the sweet-smelling urine gives the disease its name.

questions.question: Homocystinuria, associated with a marfanoid habitus, lens dislocation, and thromboembolism, most commonly results from a deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Classic homocystinuria is most often caused by deficiency of cystathionine beta-synthase, a pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent enzyme that condenses homocysteine with serine to form cystathionine in the transsulfuration pathway; its block raises plasma homocysteine and methionine.

questions.question: Ammonia is particularly toxic to the brain in part because excess ammonia drives glutamate toward glutamine via glutamine synthetase, which:
options: Increases neurotransmitter glutamate availability, causing overstimulation
Depletes alpha-ketoglutarate (drawn off to replenish glutamate), impairing TCA cycle flux and cellular energy production in astrocytes
Has no metabolic consequence for astrocytes
questions.correct_answer: Depletes alpha-ketoglutarate (drawn off to replenish glutamate), impairing TCA cycle flux and cellular energy production in astrocytes
questions.explanation: Hyperammonemia drives glutamate dehydrogenase toward glutamate formation and glutamine synthetase toward glutamine formation in astrocytes, depleting alpha-ketoglutarate and glutamate, impairing TCA cycle function and ATP production, and also causing astrocyte swelling (osmotic effect of glutamine) — central to ammonia's neurotoxicity.

questions.question: Protein turnover in the cytosol, particularly for short-lived and misfolded proteins, is primarily carried out by the:
questions.explanation: Proteins targeted for rapid, regulated degradation are tagged with polyubiquitin chains (via E1-E2-E3 enzyme cascades) and degraded by the 26S proteasome, the major pathway for cytosolic and nuclear protein turnover.

questions.question: Long-lived proteins and whole organelles are degraded mainly via which pathway, distinct from the ubiquitin-proteasome system?
questions.explanation: Long-lived cytosolic proteins and organelles are engulfed by autophagosomes and delivered to lysosomes for bulk degradation by cathepsins, complementing the more selective, rapid ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.

questions.question: A healthy adult in nitrogen balance excretes nitrogen (mainly as urea) at a rate that:
options: Is always zero regardless of intake
Bears no relationship to dietary intake
questions.explanation: Nitrogen balance describes the state where nitrogen intake (chiefly from dietary protein) equals nitrogen output (urine, feces, skin); healthy adults are typically in zero nitrogen balance, whereas growing children or pregnant women are in positive balance.

questions.question: A patient in negative nitrogen balance, where nitrogen excretion exceeds intake, is most consistent with:
options: Growth, pregnancy, or tissue repair (anabolic states)
Starvation, severe burns, trauma, or wasting illness (catabolic states)
questions.correct_answer: Starvation, severe burns, trauma, or wasting illness (catabolic states)
questions.explanation: Negative nitrogen balance occurs when tissue protein breakdown exceeds synthesis and intake, as in starvation, severe illness, burns, or trauma, reflecting net loss of body protein.

questions.question: Which of the following is classified as an essential amino acid that must be supplied in the human diet?
questions.explanation: Lysine is one of the nine standard essential amino acids in humans (histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine) that cannot be synthesized de novo and must come from the diet.

questions.question: Non-essential amino acids are, by definition, those that:
options: Are not used in protein synthesis
Can be synthesized by the body in sufficient quantity from other metabolic precursors, so dietary intake is not strictly required
Are only found in plant proteins
questions.correct_answer: Can be synthesized by the body in sufficient quantity from other metabolic precursors, so dietary intake is not strictly required
questions.explanation: Non-essential amino acids (e.g., alanine, aspartate, glutamate, serine, glycine) can be synthesized endogenously from common metabolic intermediates via transamination or other pathways, so they need not be obtained from the diet under normal conditions.

questions.question: Tyrosine and cysteine are termed 'conditionally essential' amino acids because:
options: They are always essential regardless of physiological state
They are normally synthesizable from phenylalanine and methionine respectively, but become dietary requirements if the precursor's metabolism is impaired or supply is inadequate
They are never used by the body
They can only be obtained from animal sources
questions.correct_answer: They are normally synthesizable from phenylalanine and methionine respectively, but become dietary requirements if the precursor's metabolism is impaired or supply is inadequate
questions.explanation: Tyrosine (from phenylalanine via phenylalanine hydroxylase) and cysteine (from methionine via the transsulfuration pathway) are normally non-essential but become 'conditionally essential' when their precursor amino acid or the relevant enzyme is limited, as in PKU or liver disease.

questions.question: The first step in heme biosynthesis, condensation of glycine and succinyl-CoA to form delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), is catalyzed by ALA synthase and requires which coenzyme?
questions.explanation: ALA synthase, the rate-limiting mitochondrial enzyme of heme synthesis, requires pyridoxal phosphate as coenzyme to condense glycine with succinyl-CoA, forming delta-aminolevulinic acid, illustrating an amino acid (glycine) serving as a biosynthetic precursor beyond protein synthesis.

questions.question: S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the principal biological methyl-group donor for reactions such as creatine, epinephrine, and phosphatidylcholine synthesis, is formed from which amino acid?
questions.explanation: Methionine adenosyltransferase combines methionine with ATP to form S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the universal methyl donor used in numerous biosynthetic methylation reactions throughout the body.

questions.question: Creatine, important for the phosphocreatine energy buffer in muscle, is synthesized from which three amino acids?
questions.explanation: Creatine synthesis begins with transfer of arginine's amidino group to glycine (forming guanidinoacetate), which is then methylated by SAM (derived from methionine) to form creatine.

questions.question: Tryptophan serves as the metabolic precursor for which important neurotransmitter and, subsequently, the hormone melatonin?
questions.explanation: Tryptophan is hydroxylated and decarboxylated to form serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine), which is further metabolized to melatonin in the pineal gland; tryptophan is also a precursor of the vitamin niacin.

questions.question: Overall, the four principal fates of the carbon skeletons of catabolized amino acids are that they can be converted to:
options: Pyruvate, acetyl-CoA/acetoacetyl-CoA, or one of the TCA cycle intermediates (alpha-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, fumarate, oxaloacetate)
questions.correct_answer: Pyruvate, acetyl-CoA/acetoacetyl-CoA, or one of the TCA cycle intermediates (alpha-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, fumarate, oxaloacetate)
questions.explanation: After removal of the amino group, the 20 standard amino acids' carbon skeletons funnel into central metabolism at one of seven points: pyruvate, acetyl-CoA, acetoacetyl-CoA, alpha-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, fumarate, or oxaloacetate, determining their glucogenic and/or ketogenic classification.
